claim: Larval zebrafish swim trajectories in homogeneous environments are characterized by alternating sequences of repeated turns to the left and to the right.
source: We mapped the structure of larval zebrafish swim trajectories in homogeneous environments and found that trajectories were characterized by alternating sequences of repeated turns to the left and to the right.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by experimental data from freely swimming fish showing turn sequences and streak patterns (Figure 1B-F).

claim: The anterior rhombencephalic turning region (ARTR) is a neural population whose activity relates to spontaneous turning behavior.
source: Using whole-brain light-sheet imaging, we identified activity relating to the behavior in specific neural populations that we termed the anterior rhombencephalic turning region (ARTR).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-brain imaging data showing correlation between ARTR activity and turning behavior (Figure 2).

claim: ARTR perturbations bias swim direction.
source: ARTR perturbations biased swim direction and reduced the dependence of turn direction on turn history, indicating that the ARTR is part of a network generating the temporal correlations in turn direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by laser ablation and optogenetic stimulation experiments showing changes in turn bias (Figure 4).

claim: ARTR perturbations reduce the dependence of turn direction on turn history.
source: ARTR perturbations biased swim direction and reduced the dependence of turn direction on turn history, indicating that the ARTR is part of a network generating the temporal correlations in turn direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of streak length distributions before and after ARTR ablation (Figure 4D-G).

claim: The ARTR is part of a network generating temporal correlations in turn direction.
source: ARTR perturbations biased swim direction and reduced the dependence of turn direction on turn history, indicating that the ARTR is part of a network generating the temporal correlations in turn direction.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the ablation experiments showing reduced temporal correlations after ARTR lesions.

claim: There is suggestive evidence for ARTR mutual inhibition.
source: We also find suggestive evidence for ARTR mutual inhibition and ARTR projections to premotor neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on anatomical tracing showing GABAergic lateral ARTR clusters project contralaterally (Figure 5B).

claim: There is suggestive evidence for ARTR projections to premotor neurons.
source: We also find suggestive evidence for ARTR mutual inhibition and ARTR projections to premotor neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on anatomical tracing showing medial ARTR projections near reticulospinal neurons (Figure 5D).

claim: The observed turn sequences may underlie efficient exploration of local environments.
source: Finally, simulations suggest the observed turn sequences may underlie efficient exploration of local environments.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling comparing correlated vs. random turning strategies (Figure 6).

claim: Fish execute discrete spontaneous turns at an average rate of one bout every 1.22 ± 0.16 s.
source: Because larval zebrafish swim in discrete swim bouts (Figure 1A, right; on average one bout every 1.22 ± 0.16 s, mean ± SEM across fish), the behavior could be partitioned into a punctuated series of swim bout locations and turn angles (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by measurements from freely swimming fish.

claim: Fish string together repeated turns in one direction before stochastically switching to a chain of turns in the other direction.
source: We observed that fish do not randomly choose a turning direction, but rather string together repeated turns in one direction before stochastically switching to a chain of turns in the other direction (Figure 1B,C; Video 1; overall turn angle distribution shown in Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of turn sequences and streak lengths from behavioral data.

claim: Correlations in turn direction result in an increase in cumulative signed turn direction after a switch in turn direction that is significantly different from a random model for chains of five turns.
source: In real fish, correlations in turn direction resulted in an increase in cumulative signed turn direction after a switch in turn direction. This increase was significantly different, for chains of five turns, from that of a model fish swimming left and right randomly (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Figure 1—source data 1; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison between observed data and a random turning model.

claim: Long streaks of turns in the same direction are significantly more prevalent in real fish than in a random model, up to streaks of at least 15 turns.
source: Furthermore, histograms of streak length showed that long streaks were significantly more prevalent in the real data than in the model fish, up to streaks of at least 15 turns (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of streak length distributions.

claim: Freely swimming fish spontaneously chain together turns biased in the same direction for approximately 6 seconds on average.
source: We conclude that freely swimming fish spontaneously chain together turns biased in the same direction for approximately 6 seconds on average (assuming 1.2 seconds/bout) and much longer in some periods (45% of bouts are in streaks of 5 bouts or longer; 14% in streaks of 10 bouts or longer; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C), significantly deviating from a random walk (Codling et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of turn sequences and streak durations from behavioral data.

claim: 45% of swim bouts are in streaks of 5 bouts or longer.
source: We conclude that freely swimming fish spontaneously chain together turns biased in the same direction for approximately 6 seconds on average (assuming 1.2 seconds/bout) and much longer in some periods (45% of bouts are in streaks of 5 bouts or longer; 14% in streaks of 10 bouts or longer; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C), significantly deviating from a random walk (Codling et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by analysis of streak length distributions.

claim: 14% of swim bouts are in streaks of 10 bouts or longer.
source: We conclude that freely swimming fish spontaneously chain together turns biased in the same direction for approximately 6 seconds on average (assuming 1.2 seconds/bout) and much longer in some periods (45% of bouts are in streaks of 5 bouts or longer; 14% in streaks of 10 bouts or longer; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C), significantly deviating from a random walk (Codling et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by analysis of streak length distributions.

claim: Freely swimming fish significantly deviate from a random walk.
source: We conclude that freely swimming fish spontaneously chain together turns biased in the same direction for approximately 6 seconds on average (assuming 1.2 seconds/bout) and much longer in some periods (45% of bouts are in streaks of 5 bouts or longer; 14% in streaks of 10 bouts or longer; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C), significantly deviating from a random walk (Codling et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison to random walk models and cites established literature on random walks.

claim: Fictively behaving zebrafish exhibit behavioral sequences similar to freely swimming zebrafish, with similar chains of unilateral turns.
source: We confirmed that fictively behaving zebrafish exhibit behavioral sequences similar to freely swimming zebrafish, with similar chains of unilateral turns (compare Figure 1H–L to Figure 1B–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of behavioral statistics between freely swimming and fictively swimming fish.

claim: The fictive swim frequency was slightly slower relative to freely swimming conditions (modefictive/modefree = 1.4; meanfictive/meanfree = 2.4; medianfictive/medianfree = 1.9).
source: While the fictive swim frequency was slightly slower relative to freely swimming conditions (modefictive/modefree = 1.4; meanfictive/meanfree = 2.4; medianfictive/medianfree = 1.9), the large overlap between the histograms of inter-bout intervals (IBIs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C) suggests that fictive behavior is sufficiently similar to that of freely swimming fish to allow for analysis of concurrent neural signals.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative comparison of swim frequencies between conditions.

claim: There is large overlap between the histograms of inter-bout intervals for fictive and freely swimming fish.
source: While the fictive swim frequency was slightly slower relative to freely swimming conditions (modefictive/modefree = 1.4; meanfictive/meanfree = 2.4; medianfictive/medianfree = 1.9), the large overlap between the histograms of inter-bout intervals (IBIs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C) suggests that fictive behavior is sufficiently similar to that of freely swimming fish to allow for analysis of concurrent neural signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of IBI distributions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Fictive behavior is sufficiently similar to that of freely swimming fish to allow for analysis of concurrent neural signals.
source: While the fictive swim frequency was slightly slower relative to freely swimming conditions (modefictive/modefree = 1.4; meanfictive/meanfree = 2.4; medianfictive/medianfree = 1.9), the large overlap between the histograms of inter-bout intervals (IBIs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C) suggests that fictive behavior is sufficiently similar to that of freely swimming fish to allow for analysis of concurrent neural signals.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the similarity of behavioral statistics between conditions.

claim: Whole-brain imaging captured activity at 1.87 ± 0.14 brain volumes per second during spontaneous behavior.
source: Using transgenic zebrafish expressing the genetically encoded calcium indicator GCaMP6f or GCaMP6s (Chen et al., 2013) in most neurons ('Materials and methods'), and a dual-laser light-sheet microscope capable of scanning the entire brain without exposing the retina to the laser beam (Vladimirov et al., 2014) (Figure 2A), we captured whole-brain neuron-resolution activity at 1.87 ± 0.14 (mean ± SD over all recordings) brain volumes per second during spontaneous behavior (Video 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by technical specifications of the imaging system.

claim: The most spatially conserved functionally defined cell clusters across fish were in a region in the anterior hindbrain.
source: Anatomical consistency of the functionally identified regions was evaluated using a nonlinear volume registration algorithm (Portugues et al., 2014) that aligned seven brains based only on anatomy; this analysis revealed that, across fish, the most spatially conserved functionally defined cell clusters were in a region in the anterior hindbrain (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by registration analysis across multiple fish brains.

claim: The anterior hindbrain region is composed of two bilaterally symmetric clusters of cells on either side of the midline.
source: This region is composed of two bilaterally symmetric clusters of cells on either side of the midline.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical observations from imaging data.

claim: The dynamics of ARTR cells were tightly coupled to the direction of turning and highly antiphasic.
source: The dynamics of these cells were tightly coupled to the direction of turning and highly antiphasic, such that the majority of the time, cells in only one hemisphere were active (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by time series analysis of ARTR activity during turning behavior.

claim: The majority of the time, cells in only one ARTR hemisphere were active.
source: The dynamics of these cells were tightly coupled to the direction of turning and highly antiphasic, such that the majority of the time, cells in only one hemisphere were active (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation of antiphasic activity patterns in imaging data.

claim: There are 60 ± 7 neurons in each medial ARTR cluster.
source: We manually counted the numbers of neurons in the functional brain maps and found 60 ± 7 neurons in each medial cluster and 33 ± 2 neurons in each lateral cluster (mean ± SEM, 8 fish).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by manual cell counting from imaging data.

claim: There are 33 ± 2 neurons in each lateral ARTR cluster.
source: We manually counted the numbers of neurons in the functional brain maps and found 60 ± 7 neurons in each medial cluster and 33 ± 2 neurons in each lateral cluster (mean ± SEM, 8 fish).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by manual cell counting from imaging data.

claim: At the time of a turn, the ipsilateral ARTR was activated.
source: At the time of a turn, the ipsilateral ARTR was activated, and after a rise in calcium signal over about 2 s, decayed to baseline slowly on a timescale of 5–10 s (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by turn-triggered averaging of ARTR activity.

claim: After a turn, ARTR calcium signal rises over about 2 s and then decays to baseline slowly on a timescale of 5–10 s.
source: At the time of a turn, the ipsilateral ARTR was activated, and after a rise in calcium signal over about 2 s, decayed to baseline slowly on a timescale of 5–10 s (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of ARTR temporal dynamics from imaging data.

claim: The most prominent directionally tuned neurons were located in the hindbrain.
source: These averaged functional brain maps (Figure 3A–B) revealed that the most prominent directionally tuned neurons were located in the hindbrain, where most tuning was ipsilateral to turning direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of averaged functional brain maps across fish.

claim: Most directional tuning in the hindbrain was ipsilateral to turning direction.
source: These averaged functional brain maps (Figure 3A–B) revealed that the most prominent directionally tuned neurons were located in the hindbrain, where most tuning was ipsilateral to turning direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of directional tuning patterns in functional maps.

claim: Prominent directionally tuned neurons were found in the ARTR in rhombomeres 2–3, diffusely distributed in rhombomeres 4–6, in the inferior olive, and in the vicinity of and overlapping with the reticulospinal system.
source: These prominent directionally tuned neurons were found in the ARTR in rhombomeres 2–3, diffusely distributed in rhombomeres 4–6 (Rh4-6), in the inferior olive (IO), and in the vicinity of and overlapping with the reticulospinal system (Figure 3C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical localization of functionally identified neurons.

claim: Weaker and less directionally tuned signals were observed in the torus longitudinalis, the habenula, the preoptic area and pretectum, the cerebellum, and the midbrain tegmentum, including the area containing the nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus.
source: Weaker and less directionally tuned signals were observed in the torus longitudinalis, the habenula, the preoptic area and pretectum, the cerebellum (Cb, Figure 3D), and the midbrain tegmentum, including the area containing the nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (nMLF, Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of functional signals across different brain regions.

claim: The ARTR is more directionally tuned than Rh4-6.
source: Directly comparing the directional tuning of the ARTR and Rh4-6, however, revealed that the ARTR was more directionally tuned (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison of tuning indices between regions.

claim: The ARTR is more predictive of future turn direction than Rh4-6.
source: In addition, the ARTR was more predictive of future turn direction (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis comparing predictive power of different regions.

claim: The ARTR has slower dynamics than Rh4-6.
source: In addition, we compared the temporal dynamics of the ARTR and Rh4-6 and found that the ARTR had slower dynamics than Rh4-6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C), suggesting that the ARTR may be more involved in the slow dynamics of the behavior and Rh4-6 more in direct behavioral output.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of temporal response profiles of the two regions.

claim: The ARTR may be more involved in the slow dynamics of the behavior and Rh4-6 more in direct behavioral output.
source: In addition, we compared the temporal dynamics of the ARTR and Rh4-6 and found that the ARTR had slower dynamics than Rh4-6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C), suggesting that the ARTR may be more involved in the slow dynamics of the behavior and Rh4-6 more in direct behavioral output.
evidence: This claim is speculative inference based on the observed differences in temporal dynamics.

claim: The inferior olive projects only to the contralateral cerebellum.
source: Further, while the IO was strongly directionally tuned, it projects only to the contralateral Cb (De Zeeuw et al., 1998; Bae et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: Directional tuning with flipped laterality was observed in the cerebellum.
source: While we did see directional tuning with flipped laterality in the Cb (Figure 3D), this signal was only weakly tuned to behavior, and therefore, the IO-Cb circuit may be less directly related to turn patterns.
evidence: This claim is supported by observation of tuning patterns in the cerebellum from imaging data.

claim: The cerebellar signal was only weakly tuned to behavior.
source: While we did see directional tuning with flipped laterality in the Cb (Figure 3D), this signal was only weakly tuned to behavior, and therefore, the IO-Cb circuit may be less directly related to turn patterns.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of tuning strength in the cerebellum.

claim: The IO-Cb circuit may be less directly related to turn patterns.
source: While we did see directional tuning with flipped laterality in the Cb (Figure 3D), this signal was only weakly tuned to behavior, and therefore, the IO-Cb circuit may be less directly related to turn patterns.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the weak tuning observed in the cerebellum.

claim: After unilateral ARTR ablation, fish turned relatively more often toward the direction of the intact half of the ARTR (shift in turn direction to intact side: 18 ± 4%).
source: We found that post-ablation, fish turned relatively more often toward the direction of the intact half of the ARTR (shift in turn direction to intact side: 18 ± 4%, mean ± SEM; Figure 4A–B) (left ARTR ablation: N = 6 fish, p=0.031; right ARTR ablation: N = 7 fish, p=0.031; sham ablation: N = 5, p=0.438, paired signed rank test), suggesting that the ARTR is involved in generating directionality bias in spontaneous turning behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral measurements before and after ablation experiments.

claim: Left ARTR ablation significantly changes turn bias (N = 6 fish, p=0.031).
source: We found that post-ablation, fish turned relatively more often toward the direction of the intact half of the ARTR (shift in turn direction to intact side: 18 ± 4%, mean ± SEM; Figure 4A–B) (left ARTR ablation: N = 6 fish, p=0.031; right ARTR ablation: N = 7 fish, p=0.031; sham ablation: N = 5, p=0.438, paired signed rank test), suggesting that the ARTR is involved in generating directionality bias in spontaneous turning behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ablation experiment results.

claim: Right ARTR ablation significantly changes turn bias (N = 7 fish, p=0.031).
source: We found that post-ablation, fish turned relatively more often toward the direction of the intact half of the ARTR (shift in turn direction to intact side: 18 ± 4%, mean ± SEM; Figure 4A–B) (left ARTR ablation: N = 6 fish, p=0.031; right ARTR ablation: N = 7 fish, p=0.031; sham ablation: N = 5, p=0.438, paired signed rank test), suggesting that the ARTR is involved in generating directionality bias in spontaneous turning behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ablation experiment results.

claim: Sham ablation does not significantly change turn bias (N = 5, p=0.438).
source: We found that post-ablation, fish turned relatively more often toward the direction of the intact half of the ARTR (shift in turn direction to intact side: 18 ± 4%, mean ± SEM; Figure 4A–B) (left ARTR ablation: N = 6 fish, p=0.031; right ARTR ablation: N = 7 fish, p=0.031; sham ablation: N = 5, p=0.438, paired signed rank test), suggesting that the ARTR is involved in generating directionality bias in spontaneous turning behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of control ablation experiments.

claim: The ARTR is involved in generating directionality bias in spontaneous turning behavior.
source: We found that post-ablation, fish turned relatively more often toward the direction of the intact half of the ARTR (shift in turn direction to intact side: 18 ± 4%, mean ± SEM; Figure 4A–B) (left ARTR ablation: N = 6 fish, p=0.031; right ARTR ablation: N = 7 fish, p=0.031; sham ablation: N = 5, p=0.438, paired signed rank test), suggesting that the ARTR is involved in generating directionality bias in spontaneous turning behavior.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the results of ablation experiments.

claim: After ARTR ablation, the magnitude of turns to either the ablated or intact side remained unchanged.
source: In contrast to the effect of reticulospinal neuron ablation (Orger et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2013; Kimmel et al., 1982), after ARTR ablation, the magnitude of turns to either the ablated or intact side remained unchanged (Figure 4C, p=0.147, ablated side; p=0.127, intact side, N = 13 fish, paired signed rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of turn magnitudes before and after ablation.

claim: The ARTR is involved in regulating the choice of turning direction, rather than mediating the actual turn kinematics.
source: These results suggest that the ARTR is involved in regulating the choice of turning direction, rather than mediating the actual turn kinematics.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that turn magnitude is unchanged after ablation while turn bias is affected.

claim: After ARTR ablation, turn sequences in lesioned fish are more similar to strings of biased coin flips than are turn sequences in intact fish.
source: Specifically, comparing the goodness-of-fit between the matched biased random walks and the observed turn sequences ('Materials and methods'), we found a significant reduction in the normalized root-mean-square error over fish after ablation (Figure 4G, p=0.027, paired signed rank test, N = 13 fish).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of streak distributions to random models.

claim: There is a significant reduction in the normalized root-mean-square error comparing turn sequences to random models after ARTR ablation (p=0.027, N = 13 fish).
source: Specifically, comparing the goodness-of-fit between the matched biased random walks and the observed turn sequences ('Materials and methods'), we found a significant reduction in the normalized root-mean-square error over fish after ablation (Figure 4G, p=0.027, paired signed rank test, N = 13 fish).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The ARTR is part of a circuit that implements a temporally correlated process.
source: These results indicate that turn sequences in lesioned fish are more similar to strings of biased coin flips than are turn sequences in intact fish, providing evidence that the ARTR is part of a circuit that implements a temporally correlated process.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the change in temporal structure after ablation.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of ARTR cells causes an increase in the number of turns in the direction ipsilateral to the stimulated ARTR region (29 ± 9% shift).
source: Stimulating ARTR cells caused an increase in the number of turns in the direction ipsilateral to the stimulated ARTR region (Figure 4H–K; 29 ± 9%, mean ± SEM, shift in turns to the stimulated direction; left stimulation, p=0.004; right stimulation, p=0.002, paired signed rank test, N = 7 fish), independent of whether the medial clusters or lateral clusters were chosen for stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral measurements during optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: Left ARTR optogenetic stimulation significantly increases ipsilateral turns (p=0.004, N = 7 fish).
source: Stimulating ARTR cells caused an increase in the number of turns in the direction ipsilateral to the stimulated ARTR region (Figure 4H–K; 29 ± 9%, mean ± SEM, shift in turns to the stimulated direction; left stimulation, p=0.004; right stimulation, p=0.002, paired signed rank test, N = 7 fish), independent of whether the medial clusters or lateral clusters were chosen for stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of optogenetic stimulation results.

claim: Right ARTR optogenetic stimulation significantly increases ipsilateral turns (p=0.002, N = 7 fish).
source: Stimulating ARTR cells caused an increase in the number of turns in the direction ipsilateral to the stimulated ARTR region (Figure 4H–K; 29 ± 9%, mean ± SEM, shift in turns to the stimulated direction; left stimulation, p=0.004; right stimulation, p=0.002, paired signed rank test, N = 7 fish), independent of whether the medial clusters or lateral clusters were chosen for stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of optogenetic stimulation results.

claim: The effect of ARTR stimulation on turn bias is independent of whether the medial clusters or lateral clusters were chosen for stimulation.
source: Stimulating ARTR cells caused an increase in the number of turns in the direction ipsilateral to the stimulated ARTR region (Figure 4H–K; 29 ± 9%, mean ± SEM, shift in turns to the stimulated direction; left stimulation, p=0.004; right stimulation, p=0.002, paired signed rank test, N = 7 fish), independent of whether the medial clusters or lateral clusters were chosen for stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of stimulation effects across different ARTR clusters.

claim: The ARTR is functionally connected to downstream motor circuitry.
source: These results are corroborated by electrical stimulation experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D), demonstrating that the ARTR is functionally connected to downstream motor circuitry and that activity in the ARTR influences turn direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrical stimulation experiments showing behavioral effects.

claim: Activity in the ARTR influences turn direction.
source: These results are corroborated by electrical stimulation experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D), demonstrating that the ARTR is functionally connected to downstream motor circuitry and that activity in the ARTR influences turn direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by both optogenetic and electrical stimulation experiments.

claim: The magnitude of turns during stimulation of the medial ARTR clusters tends to increase.
source: In contrast to our ablation results, the magnitude of turns during stimulation of the medial clusters tended to increase (Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, left stimulation, p=0.010; right stimulation, p=0.036, paired signed rank test, N = 7 fish), indicating that either the ARTR is able to bias turn magnitude in addition to turn direction, or that there is a spillover of artificial ARTR stimulation to downstream circuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of turn magnitudes during stimulation.

claim: Either the ARTR is able to bias turn magnitude in addition to turn direction, or there is a spillover of artificial ARTR stimulation to downstream circuits.
source: In contrast to our ablation results, the magnitude of turns during stimulation of the medial clusters tended to increase (Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, left stimulation, p=0.010; right stimulation, p=0.036, paired signed rank test, N = 7 fish), indicating that either the ARTR is able to bias turn magnitude in addition to turn direction, or that there is a spillover of artificial ARTR stimulation to downstream circuits.
evidence: This claim is speculative inference to explain the difference between ablation and stimulation results.

claim: The medial clusters of the ARTR are glutamatergic.
source: In this way, the medial clusters of the ARTR were identified as being glutamatergic, and the lateral clusters as being primarily GABAergic (Figure 5A middle and right, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap with vglut2a expression in double transgenic fish.

claim: The lateral clusters of the ARTR are primarily GABAergic.
source: In this way, the medial clusters of the ARTR were identified as being glutamatergic, and the lateral clusters as being primarily GABAergic (Figure 5A middle and right, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap with gad1b expression in double transgenic fish.

claim: Neurites from the lateral GABAergic clusters reach across the midline toward both contralateral ARTR clusters.
source: Indeed, tracing PA-GFP-activated neurites from the lateral GABAergic clusters revealed projections reaching across the midline toward both contralateral ARTR clusters (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical tracing using photoactivatable GFP.

claim: Neurites from the medial glutamatergic clusters do not cross the midline.
source: In contrast, we did not find evidence for neurites from the medial glutamatergic clusters crossing the midline (Figure 5B, bottom right).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical tracing showing absence of contralateral projections from medial clusters.

claim: The ARTR anatomy is suggestive of a mutually inhibitory circuit motif.
source: Although these tracing studies cannot prove whether there exists synaptic connectivity between the ARTR clusters, they are suggestive of a mutually inhibitory circuit motif, which could mediate the antiphasic activation necessary for patterning directional motor output.
evidence: This claim is speculative inference based on the observed projection patterns and neurotransmitter identities.

claim: A mutually inhibitory circuit motif could mediate the antiphasic activation necessary for patterning directional motor output.
source: Although these tracing studies cannot prove whether there exists synaptic connectivity between the ARTR clusters, they are suggestive of a mutually inhibitory circuit motif, which could mediate the antiphasic activation necessary for patterning directional motor output.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about potential circuit function based on observed anatomy.

claim: Some labeled neurites from the medial ARTR cluster terminate in the inferior olive.
source: Photoactivation of the medial ARTR cluster revealed that while some labeled neurites terminated in the IO (Figure 5C), projections also descended into the MLF and were visible adjacent to reticulospinal neurons RoV3 and RoM3 (Figure 5D), of which RoV3 has been shown to be directionally tuned during the optomotor response (Orger et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical tracing showing projections to the IO.

claim: Projections from the medial ARTR cluster descend into the MLF and are visible adjacent to reticulospinal neurons RoV3 and RoM3.
source: Photoactivation of the medial ARTR cluster revealed that while some labeled neurites terminated in the IO (Figure 5C), projections also descended into the MLF and were visible adjacent to reticulospinal neurons RoV3 and RoM3 (Figure 5D), of which RoV3 has been shown to be directionally tuned during the optomotor response (Orger et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical tracing showing projections near reticulospinal neurons.

claim: RoV3 has been shown to be directionally tuned during the optomotor response.
source: Photoactivation of the medial ARTR cluster revealed that while some labeled neurites terminated in the IO (Figure 5C), projections also descended into the MLF and were visible adjacent to reticulospinal neurons RoV3 and RoM3 (Figure 5D), of which RoV3 has been shown to be directionally tuned during the optomotor response (Orger et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from a cited previous study.

claim: Both ARTR and vSPN neurons are directionally tuned.
source: We also looked at differences in temporal dynamics between ARTR activity and vSPN activity. We found that both sets of neurons were directionally tuned (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), but that the ARTR exhibited slower dynamics in the fluorescence signal than the vSPNs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of tuning properties from imaging data.

claim: The ARTR exhibits slower dynamics in the fluorescence signal than the vSPNs.
source: We also looked at differences in temporal dynamics between ARTR activity and vSPN activity. We found that both sets of neurons were directionally tuned (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), but that the ARTR exhibited slower dynamics in the fluorescence signal than the vSPNs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of temporal response profiles between regions.

claim: The ARTR is also activated during the optomotor response.
source: We also tested whether ARTR neurons are exclusively activated during spontaneous turning or also during visually driven behaviors and found that the ARTR is also activated during the optomotor response (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting that this brain area subserves multiple behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data during visual stimulation experiments.

claim: The ARTR subserves multiple behaviors.
source: We also tested whether ARTR neurons are exclusively activated during spontaneous turning or also during visually driven behaviors and found that the ARTR is also activated during the optomotor response (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting that this brain area subserves multiple behaviors.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on ARTR activation during both spontaneous and visually-driven behaviors.

claim: Correlated directional locomotion results in a unique spatial pattern over time.
source: Because correlated directional locomotion results in a unique spatial pattern over time, we posited that it may reflect a baseline foraging strategy when external guiding cues are scarce.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of spatial patterns in swim trajectories.

claim: Correlated turning may reflect a baseline foraging strategy when external guiding cues are scarce.
source: Because correlated directional locomotion results in a unique spatial pattern over time, we posited that it may reflect a baseline foraging strategy when external guiding cues are scarce.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the potential ethological function of the behavior.

claim: Chaotic oscillators driving autonomous agents produce winding trajectories that efficiently and evenly cover a space, without diffusing into faraway regions.
source: This idea is supported by engineering literature wherein chaotic oscillators driving autonomous agents (Tlelo-Cuautle and Ramos-López, 2014; Mobus and Fisher, 1999) produce winding trajectories that efficiently and evenly cover a space, without diffusing into faraway regions.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from cited engineering literature.

claim: A two-state Markov model with high probabilities of remaining in the same turn state produces behavior similar to that of real fish.
source: This two-state Markov model (Rabiner, 1989), which stochastically switches between a 'left turn' state and a 'right turn' state but exhibits high probabilities of remaining in the same turn state (Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, 'Materials and methods'), produced behavior similar to that of real fish (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C) based only on low-level parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model output to real behavioral data.

claim: The correlated turning strategy covers a restricted area more efficiently than a model fish turning left and right randomly without turn history dependence.
source: Using this Markov model to simulate trajectories through virtual space (Figure 6B), we show that such a scheme covers a restricted area more efficiently than a model fish turning left and right randomly without turn history dependence, and reduces diffusion into faraway regions (Figure 6C–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational simulations comparing different turning strategies.

claim: The correlated turning strategy reduces diffusion into faraway regions compared to random turning.
source: Using this Markov model to simulate trajectories through virtual space (Figure 6B), we show that such a scheme covers a restricted area more efficiently than a model fish turning left and right randomly without turn history dependence, and reduces diffusion into faraway regions (Figure 6C–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational simulations comparing diffusion rates.

claim: The correlated turning strategy presents two distinct advantages: preventing rapid spatial diffusion into unknown territories and enabling efficient coverage of local areas.
source: This strategy presents two distinct advantages. First, rapid spatial diffusion may lead the fish into unknown and potentially unsafe territories; this should be prevented. Second, given this preference to remain local, covering an area efficiently in the search for food cues represents an energetically favorable program that ensures no nearby resources have been missed.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the potential adaptive value of the behavior.

claim: The ARTR is part of a circuit that implements a foraging strategy that discourages travel into uncertain territory, instead favoring efficient and even exploration of the local environment.
source: Thus, we speculate that the ARTR is part of a circuit that implements a foraging strategy that discourages travel into uncertain territory, instead favoring efficient and even exploration of the local environment.
evidence: This claim is speculative synthesis of the experimental and modeling results.

claim: The ARTR contributes to the control of correlations in turn direction by biasing turn direction through subthreshold excitation of reticulospinal neurons by the medial cluster of cells.
source: We hypothesize that the ARTR contributes to the control of correlations in turn direction according to the following mechanism. Activity on one side of the ARTR biases turn direction by subthreshold excitation of reticulospinal neurons by the medial cluster of cells.
evidence: This claim is a hypothetical mechanism proposed to explain the observed phenomena.

claim: When the fish turns in the direction where the ARTR is active, a motor copy feeds back on the ipsilateral ARTR and re-activates it.
source: When the fish turns in the direction where the ARTR is active, a motor copy feeds back on the ipsilateral ARTR and re-activates it, which also suppresses the contralateral ARTR through contralateral inhibition.
evidence: This claim is a hypothetical mechanism proposed to explain the observed temporal dynamics.

claim: ARTR re-activation suppresses the contralateral ARTR through contralateral inhibition.
source: When the fish turns in the direction where the ARTR is active, a motor copy feeds back on the ipsilateral ARTR and re-activates it, which also suppresses the contralateral ARTR through contralateral inhibition.
evidence: This claim is a hypothetical mechanism based on the observed antiphasic activity and anatomical projections.

claim: ARTR activity decays slowly, biasing turns to the same direction.
source: Next, ARTR activity decays slowly, again biasing turns to the same direction.
evidence: This claim is based on observed temporal dynamics of ARTR activity.

claim: Switches in turn direction might arise from spontaneous activity in the ARTR population, from spontaneous or evoked input from neurons upstream of the ARTR, or when ARTR activity has decayed sufficiently.
source: Switches in turn direction might arise from spontaneous activity in the ARTR population, from spontaneous or evoked input from neurons upstream of the ARTR, or when ARTR activity has decayed sufficiently so that it no longer exerts a bias on turning direction.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms for state switching.

claim: Comprehensive, whole-brain, cell-level imaging was crucial for discovering the ARTR circuit.
source: Comprehensive, whole-brain, cell-level imaging was crucial for discovering the ARTR circuit (Vladimirov et al., 2014; Freeman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on the methodological approach used in the study and cites relevant technical papers.

claim: Lacking a priori hypotheses regarding the location of circuits governing a behavior, near-complete coverage helps ensure that neurons with response properties of interest will likely be identified.
source: Lacking a priori hypotheses regarding the location of circuits governing a behavior, the near-complete coverage of this approach helps ensure that neurons with response properties of interest, if present, will likely be identified (depending on the sensitivity of the activity reporter [Chen et al., 2013] and the design of computational approaches [Freeman et al., 2014]).
evidence: This claim is reasoning about the advantages of the whole-brain imaging approach, citing relevant technical papers.

claim: The identified ARTR cells are likely to be the primary set of neurons consistently involved in generating directional behavior.
source: Thus, while inputs to the identified neural populations certainly shape circuit activity, our measurements and analyses suggest that the identified cells are likely to be the primary set of neurons consistently involved in generating directional behavior.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the stereotypy and functional properties of the ARTR across fish.

claim: The ARTR may be part of a larger circuit performing the operation of generating temporal structure in spontaneous turn sequences.
source: However, the ARTR may also be part of a larger circuit performing this operation.
evidence: This claim acknowledges the possibility of additional circuit components beyond the ARTR.

claim: Differences between real and tethered behaviors are usually present but are, in many cases, small enough to allow for the study of related neural activity.
source: Differences between real and tethered behaviors are usually present (Dombeck and Reiser, 2012), but are, in many cases, small enough to allow for the study of related neural activity, including for relatively complex phenomena such as spatial representations (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Harvey et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from cited studies on tethered preparations.

claim: The essential properties of the turning behavior persist in fictive conditions, allowing the underlying signals to be analyzed.
source: Here, we observed differences between the fictive behavior and freely swimming behavior, such as an approximately 1.4- to 2.4-fold difference in swim frequency, but these differences were modest enough for the essential properties of the behavior to persist, allowing the underlying signals to be analyzed.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of behavioral statistics between freely swimming and fictive conditions.

claim: The initiation of locomotion in lamprey, salamander, and cat has been attributed to the mesencephalic locomotor region.
source: The initiation of locomotion in other animals, such as lamprey (Sirota et al., 2000), salamander (Cabelguen et al., 2003), and cat (Shik et al., 1969), has been attributed to the mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from cited studies in other species.

claim: The MLR has yet to be identified in the larval zebrafish.
source: While the MLR has yet to be identified in the larval zebrafish (Severi et al., 2014), the midbrain tegmental nMLF has been shown to regulate swimming (Severi et al., 2014; Thiele et al., 2014; Wang and McLean, 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on the current state of knowledge in the field, citing relevant studies.

claim: The midbrain tegmental nMLF has been shown to regulate swimming in larval zebrafish.
source: While the MLR has yet to be identified in the larval zebrafish (Severi et al., 2014), the midbrain tegmental nMLF has been shown to regulate swimming (Severi et al., 2014; Thiele et al., 2014; Wang and McLean, 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: The nMLF is routinely correlated with spontaneous swimming.
source: Consistent with this, we find the nMLF to be routinely correlated with spontaneous swimming, and it is possible that the additional mesencephalic cells not part of the nMLF but correlated strongly with swim amplitude (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) may be part of the larval zebrafish MLR.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data showing nMLF activity during swimming.

claim: Additional mesencephalic cells correlated strongly with swim amplitude may be part of the larval zebrafish MLR.
source: Consistent with this, we find the nMLF to be routinely correlated with spontaneous swimming, and it is possible that the additional mesencephalic cells not part of the nMLF but correlated strongly with swim amplitude (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) may be part of the larval zebrafish MLR.
evidence: This claim is speculative inference based on the location and functional properties of observed cells.

claim: The ARTR does not initiate the command for motion but exerts a bias on the direction of swim bouts initiated by other circuits.
source: That being said, while we have reported a causal role of the ARTR in spontaneous swim patterns, we do not claim that the initial command for motion originates from the ARTR. Rather, we suggest that the ARTR exerts a bias on the direction of swim bouts initiated by other circuits.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results, particularly the lack of change in swim frequency during ARTR stimulation.

claim: The ARTR occupies a position complementary to canonical motor control centers.
source: Thus, we argue that the ARTR occupies a position complementary to canonical motor control centers.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the functional role of the ARTR in the motor control hierarchy.

claim: The neural populations uncovered by the analysis are involved in setting the direction of spontaneous swimming but may be involved in other functions as well.
source: The neural populations uncovered by our analysis are involved in setting the direction of spontaneous swimming but may be involved in other functions as well.
evidence: This claim acknowledges the possibility of multifunctional roles for the ARTR.

claim: In feature-poor environments, the ARTR system may interact with sensory systems such that ARTR control of exploration is preserved but biased by the influence of weak sensory inputs.
source: In principle, signals from other motor modalities as well as sensory systems could be integrated into ARTR activity fluctuations. In feature-poor environments, the ARTR system may interact with sensory systems in such a way that ARTR control of exploration is preserved but biased by the influence of weak sensory inputs.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about potential interactions between the ARTR and sensory systems.

claim: When stronger sensory cues are encountered, navigation systems purely driven by sensory stimulation may take over.
source: When stronger sensory cues are encountered, navigation systems purely driven by sensory stimulation may take over.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about how the ARTR might interact with sensory-driven navigation.

claim: All or part of the ARTR cell population may be involved in the optomotor response.
source: For instance, all or part of the cell population may be involved in the optomotor response, as the ARTR responds to whole-field motion, and turns in the direction of motion persist after visual stimuli disappear (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is based on observed ARTR responses to visual stimulation and persistence of turning bias.

claim: Navigational strategies during phototaxis in larval zebrafish exhibit strong temporal correlations in turning direction, potentially involving the ARTR.
source: In the context of phototaxis, navigational strategies have been observed in larval zebrafish that also exhibit strong temporal correlations in turning direction (Chen and Engert, 2014), potentially involving the ARTR.
evidence: This claim is speculative inference connecting observed phototaxis behavior to the ARTR, citing relevant literature.

claim: Eye movements and turning are correlated in larval zebrafish.
source: Furthermore, preliminary observations show that eye movements (Miri et al., 2011) and turning are correlated in larval zebrafish, and activity in the vicinity of the abducens and oculomotor nuclei is correlated to turning and ARTR activity (albeit much more weakly than the strength of correlation between the ARTR and turning, Figures 2,3).
evidence: This claim is based on preliminary observations and cites relevant literature on eye movements.

claim: Activity in the vicinity of the abducens and oculomotor nuclei is correlated to turning and ARTR activity.
source: Furthermore, preliminary observations show that eye movements (Miri et al., 2011) and turning are correlated in larval zebrafish, and activity in the vicinity of the abducens and oculomotor nuclei is correlated to turning and ARTR activity (albeit much more weakly than the strength of correlation between the ARTR and turning, Figures 2,3).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of functional imaging data in these brain regions.

claim: Multiple motor patterns may be represented in and coordinated by the ARTR.
source: Thus, it is possible that multiple motor patterns are represented in and coordinated by the ARTR.
evidence: This claim is speculative inference based on the various correlations observed between ARTR and different behaviors.

claim: The slow fluctuations in turn direction may increase foraging efficiency under the condition that the fish are restricted to a local search.
source: According to our modeling of swim trajectories generated by temporally correlated vs. uncorrelated turns, the slow fluctuations in turn direction that we observed may increase foraging efficiency under the condition that the fish are restricted to a local search (due to, for example, dangers arising from venturing into unknown places).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results comparing different turning strategies.

claim: The turning strategy may adapt to changes in the environment or internal state.
source: Future work can investigate whether this strategy adapts to changes in the environment or internal state.
evidence: This claim is a suggestion for future research based on speculation about behavioral flexibility.

claim: Food restriction or low light levels may decrease state length in order to increase diffusion and promote exploration of completely novel environments.
source: Food restriction or low light levels, for instance, may decrease state length in order to increase diffusion and promote exploration of completely novel environments.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about how the behavior might adapt to different conditions.

claim: Favorable conditions may increase state length so as to decrease the rate of diffusion while encouraging efficient sampling of the local environment.
source: Conversely, favorable conditions may increase state length so as to decrease the rate of diffusion while encouraging efficient sampling of the local environment.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about how the behavior might adapt to different conditions.

claim: The ARTR circuit is likely supported by other neurons and regions.
source: In summary, the whole-brain analysis, neural perturbation experiments and anatomical characterization together reveal a circuit contributing to the patterning of a spontaneous, self-generated behavior. While this circuit is likely supported by other neurons and regions, we speculate that its function may be to guide animals through environments where guidance from external cues is lacking, a context where animals must rely primarily on the internal drive of brain-autonomous activity.
evidence: This claim acknowledges the complexity of neural circuits and the likelihood of additional components.

claim: The function of the ARTR may be to guide animals through environments where guidance from external cues is lacking.
source: In summary, the whole-brain analysis, neural perturbation experiments and anatomical characterization together reveal a circuit contributing to the patterning of a spontaneous, self-generated behavior. While this circuit is likely supported by other neurons and regions, we speculate that its function may be to guide animals through environments where guidance from external cues is lacking, a context where animals must rely primarily on the internal drive of brain-autonomous activity.
evidence: This claim is speculative synthesis of all the experimental and modeling results to propose an ethological function.
